- Crush Utilization: BEARISH — U.S. soybean crush at 0.0% of the 8.58M bu/day installed base in 2026-07, -1.51σ against 4 prior Juls (which averaged 0.0%). For scale, the industry's ~90.0%-of-nameplate working assumption is ~86.3% restated per calendar day (it assumes ~350 operating days), and crush is seasonally lightest in late spring/summer. Plants running softer than normal for the season. Crush VOLUME can still be near a record on a bigger plant base while utilization slips — it is utilization that says whether demand is actually pulling beans. ⚠️ Crush margin is in the top third of its range (100th pctile) while utilization is soft — margins say run hard and plants are not, which points at a physical constraint (new capacity still ramping, downtime, or bean availability) rather than economics.
- Iowa holds 1.73M bu/day of the 8.58M bu/day U.S. installed base (20%), the largest of any state — so national crush economics land disproportionately on Iowa basis.
- Oil share of crush value (BOARD, oil ÷ (oil+meal) per bu at workbook yields; series: cbot:zl:front vs. cbot:zm:front): 44.8% on 2026-10-06, 100th percentile of 200 daily points since 2026-03-21 (10th–90th pctile 44.3–44.7%). Moves: 1M +0.1pts (from 44.7% on 2026-09-06); 3M +0.2pts (from 44.6% on 2026-07-07). 1-month driver: oil (oil value +1.2%/bu, meal +0.9%/bu).
- Iowa CASH oil share (series: ams:ia:oil vs. ams:ia:meal): 44.3% on 2026-10-02 (−0.5pts vs. board on 2026-10-02).
- Reading oil share: it is COMPOSITION, not margin. Rising on oil strength = the renewable-diesel pull carrying the crush; rising because meal fell = a meal glut, not demand. The higher the share, the more of crush value — and so of the domestic bid for beans — rests on the policy-set oil leg (RVO volumes, SREs, 45Z), so size policy risk to it; meal is then the byproduct, and meal export competitiveness the release valve.
